name: Kingdom of Hungary (to 1526)
summary: Founded when Stephen I was crowned in 1000; a powerful Central European kingdom that survived the Mongol invasion (1241) and peaked under Matthias Corvinus, until the Ottomans crushed it at Mohács in 1526.

location.value: The Carpathian Basin; the infobox gives 282,870 km² in 1200. The page does not state a peak extent.

terrain.value: The Great Hungarian Plain along the Danube and Tisza rivers, ringed by the Carpathian Mountains, with Lake Balaton in the west.

climate.value: Continental: hot, dry summers on the plain and cold winters, with cooler, wetter weather in the mountains.

resources.value: Gold and silver from mines at Kremnica (Körmöcbánya) and Banská Štiavnica (Selmecbánya), copper, Transylvanian salt, cattle and grain.

disasters.value: Mongol invasion killed perhaps a fifth of the people (1241–42).

population.value: About 2,000,000 people in 1200 over roughly 282,870 km² (infobox), with four or five people per km²; at least 15% died or disappeared after the Mongol invasion. This page does not cover 1500.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: German “Saxon” settlers came to Transylvania and Upper Hungary in the 1100s–1200s; Cumans settled on the plain from 1239.

economicBase.value: Wheat was the most widely produced crop, with barley also grown; the kingdom was rich in uncultivated land, silver, gold and salt.

tradeRoutes.value: Grey cattle were driven to German and Italian markets; gold, silver and copper went out through Vienna, Venice and Kraków.

wealth.value: Hungary’s mines supplied a large share of Europe’s gold in the 1300s; the royal mint at Kremnica opened around 1328.

moneyAndTax.value: The gold florin, minted from 1325 under Charles I; royal income came from mines, salt, customs and taxes on peasant households.

inequality.value: Nobles and clergy above peasants, many of them serfs.

governmentType.value: A monarchy where assemblies called Diets, summoned regularly under Andrew III, began to develop into a legislative body; the Parlamentum Generale is listed from the 1290s.

keyRulers.value: Stephen I was crowned the first king on 25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001, with a crown from Pope Sylvester II; Andrew II issued the Golden Bull in 1222; Béla IV fled to Austria after the Mongol victory at Mohi on 11 April 1241. This page covers 1000–1301 only.

succession.value: Árpád dynasty, then elected and foreign kings.

institutions.value: The Golden Bull of 1222 limited royal power and confirmed noble rights; counties and later the Diet ran local and national affairs.

stability.value: Strong under some kings but often weakened by baronial revolts, disputed successions and, after 1490, weak kings.

eliteConflict.value: Barons repeatedly challenged kings, as under Andrew II (1205–35); after 1490 the magnates dominated the weak Jagiellonian kings.

armyAndTech.value: Mounted archers early on, then armoured knights, stone castles built after 1241, and Matthias Corvinus’s paid Black Army.

majorWars.value: Mongol invasion of 1241–42, which destroyed much of the country; the embassy page says about half the population was killed or enslaved, and Béla IV then ordered stone castles built. The Ottoman victory at Mohács followed in 1526.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Hungary (checked 13 Nov 2026); Hungarian Embassy in Washington: History of Hungary (checked 14 Nov 2026) (the half-population figure is a single source and is likely rough)

territoryChange.value: Croatia came under the Hungarian crown in 1102; Matthias Corvinus later won Moravia, Silesia and, in 1485, Vienna.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included the Holy Roman Empire, Venice (over Dalmatia), Bohemia and the Ottomans; Hungary shared kings with Poland in 1370–82 and 1440–44.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded, though the first book printed in Hungary, the Chronica Hungarorum, appeared at Buda in 1473.

scienceEducation.value: Matthias Corvinus built a famous Renaissance library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana; universities were founded at Pécs (1367) and Pozsony (1460s).

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Rivers such as the Danube and Tisza carried goods; roads linked Buda to Vienna, Kraków and the Adriatic coast.

religion.value: Predominantly Roman Catholic, with Orthodox and non-Christian minorities; Stephen I adopted Catholicism as the state religion.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1301) (checked 13 Nov 2026); Hungarian Embassy in Washington: History of Hungary (checked 14 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.value: Most people spoke Hungarian; Latin was the language of the church, law and government.

artsArchitecture.value: Romanesque churches such as Ják Abbey, Gothic churches, and the Renaissance royal palaces of Matthias at Buda and Visegrád.

socialStructure.value: Magnates (barons), lesser nobles, clergy, town burghers and a large majority of peasants, many of them serfs.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the Holy Crown of St Stephen and the Catholic faith; nobles saw themselves as the Hungarian “nation”.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

ideasReligions.value: Catholic Christianity and the cult of royal saints such as Stephen, Emeric and Ladislaus; Renaissance humanism at Matthias’s court.

colonisation.value: Hungary held no overseas colonies, though its kings ruled neighbouring lands such as Croatia and parts of Dalmatia.

riseSignals.value: Founded at Christmas 1000, when Stephen I was crowned at Esztergom; the Golden Bull was issued in 1222.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Hungary (checked 13 Nov 2026); Hungarian Embassy in Washington: History of Hungary (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Stephen I founded the state in 1000 and was crowned with a crown blessed by the Pope)

declineSignals.value: Weak Jagiellonian kings after 1490, the great peasant revolt of 1514 and the Ottoman victory at Mohács (1526).
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1301); Hungarian Embassy in Washington: History of Hungary (checked 14 Nov 2026) (Mohács 1526 only)

outcome.value: After the Battle of Mohács (1526) the country was split into Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary and Transylvania. The monarchy ended with Charles IV in 1918 and the republic was formed in 1946.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Hungary (checked 13 Nov 2026); Hungarian Embassy in Washington: History of Hungary (checked 14 Nov 2026) (after Mohács (1526) the country split by about 1541 into the Hungarian Kingdom, a Habsburg part and a Turkish part; reunification took about 150 years)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
